title: Seven Nation Army
text: As a kid, Jack White misheard "Salvation Army" as "Seven Nation Army". That mix-up named a riff everyone swears is a bass. It isn't: it's a guitar through a Whammy pedal an octave down, over Meg White's pounding drums. Jack was saving it for a possible James Bond theme. He said it's about gossip around Meg, himself and the people they dated. It opened Elephant in 2003, won the Grammy for Best Rock Song, and at the 2006 World Cup Italian fans turned it into a stadium anthem.

title: Smells Like Teen Spirit
text: Kathleen Hanna wrote in marker on Kurt Cobain's wall that he smelled like Teen Spirit. He read it as a revolutionary slogan. It was a deodorant brand, the one his girlfriend Tobi Vail wore, and Cobain didn't find out until months after the single came out. He wanted to write the ultimate pop song and admitted he was trying to rip off the Pixies. Krist Novoselic called the riff ridiculous; playing it slower, Dave Grohl found the drums, with a Gap Band disco feel. It was recorded in May 1991 with Butch Vig and is the only Nevermind song credited to all three.

title: Creep
text: Thom Yorke jokingly introduced it as "our Scott Walker song" and the producers believed him: they thought it was a cover. Jonny Greenwood disliked it, finding it too soft, so he tried to ruin it: those sharp guitar blasts before the chorus are his sabotage. It came out in 1992 and flopped at first; reissued in 1993, it became a worldwide hit. Its resemblance to The Air That I Breathe, from 1972, added Albert Hammond and Mike Hazlewood to the credits. And Radiohead got so sick of it that they stopped playing it for years, until the 2016 tour.

title: Do I Wanna Know?
text: Drop the needle carefully on this groove, because here is a very fine obsession distilled in 2013. Alex Turner had one idea fixed in his head: the perspective of an R&B producer inside a four-piece rock band. That heavy, slow-walking riff comes straight from the trail they had left a year earlier with the 2012 single R U Mine. The lyrics portray a completely vulnerable guy, dragged through the paranoia of not knowing whether his partner feels the same, afraid of losing it all. It reached number 11 in the UK charts, something they hadn't managed since 2007, proof that this twist left its mark.

title: Yesterday
text: Paul McCartney woke up with the whole melody in his head, at his girlfriend's house on Wimpole Street. He was so sure he had copied it that he spent a month asking everyone whether it already existed. Meanwhile he sang it with placeholder lyrics: Scrambled Eggs. It came out on Help! in 1965, and no other Beatle plays on it: just Paul and a string quartet.

title: Wonderful Tonight
text: Some compliments are born of fascination and others are written with one eye on the clock. In 1976, Eric Clapton was waiting impatiently for Pattie Boyd to finish getting ready for the Buddy Holly party Paul McCartney was hosting. From that everyday scene of waiting, with no great artifice, came this love classic. Far from the desperate storm of Layla, the voice here lives in a clean, calm, almost domestic warmth. By telling her she looks wonderful, the line holds a double truth: genuine devotion and the comic wish to get out the door. It's the weight of simple words, the kind that turn a delay into a lifelong declaration.

title: Tiny Dancer
text: Bernie Taupin wrote these lines in 1970 thinking of Maxine Feibelman, then the band's tour seamstress and soon to be his wife. Elton John ended up setting to music a love dedication his own lyricist was carving for his fiancée, capturing the pulse of the Sunset Strip and the streets of California. The lyrics follow a girl in blue jeans mending the band's clothes among preachers and the bustle of Los Angeles. For years many listeners misheard the chorus as the name of actor Tony Danza, a funny TV slip that is now part of its legend. Released on the 1971 album Madman Across the Water, the song found a new generation in a 2000 film.

title: Sugar Man
text: It appeared in 1970 on an album called Cold Fact, by a certain Sixto Rodriguez. Dennis Coffey and Mike Theodore were behind the controls, building a mix of folk rock, psychedelia and pop that ran out of air in its own country. The release went unnoticed in American stores because the label barely reached FM radio. The lyrics portray the sidewalks of Detroit and an addict going to his dealer for a way out. It names street drugs in slang to evoke how they freeze your problems. The curious thing is that, while it sank at home, it crossed the Atlantic to become a massive phenomenon in South Africa, connecting with young people standing up to apartheid, without the author knowing anything.
